Course 02

How we learn and remember

Attention, memory, practice and study.

Lesson 4. Learning from experience

1 · Lesson

Not everything we learn is studied. Much learning happens through association and consequences. In classical conditioning, described by Pavlov, a neutral stimulus ends up triggering a response because it has been paired with another that already triggered it: the smell of a hospital can cause unease because of the times we went there in pain.

In operant conditioning, studied by Skinner, behaviour changes according to what follows it: what brings pleasant consequences tends to be repeated, and so does what allows escape from something unpleasant. This explains, for example, why avoiding what we fear brings short-term relief but keeps the fear going.

Albert Bandura added observational learning: we learn by watching others and seeing what happens to them. Children imitate, but so do adults: that is how many customs, skills and attitudes are passed on.

2 · Example

A person who felt nervous in a lift starts taking the stairs. Each time, they feel relief, and that relief reinforces the avoidance. Without realising it, they never find out that the lift is safe, and the fear persists. Exposure therapies work precisely on this mechanism.

3 · Activity

Think of a habit of yours (good or bad). Write down what sets it off (cue), what you do (behaviour) and what you get right afterwards (consequence). What would you change in the cue or the consequence to modify it?
